name: LENB
description: LENB returns the number of bytes used to represent a text string. For single-byte (ASCII) text it equals LEN; for double-byte character set (DBCS) languages such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean it counts two bytes per character.
tldr: Returns the byte length of text.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: The text or cell reference whose byte count is returned.

basicExample.explanation: Each ASCII character is one byte, so the byte count equals the character count of 5.

advancedExamples.title: DBCS text in Excel
advancedExamples.scenario: Cell A1 contains the two Chinese characters "你好" and Excel runs in a DBCS locale
advancedExamples.description: Each character counts as two bytes
advancedExamples.explanation: Under a DBCS-enabled Excel, each Chinese character is two bytes, so two characters equal 4 bytes.

advancedExamples.title: Detect double-byte content
advancedExamples.scenario: Compare LEN and LENB on mixed text
advancedExamples.description: When LENB > LEN, the string has multi-byte characters
advancedExamples.explanation: The difference reveals how many extra bytes come from multi-byte characters.

howItWorks: LENB counts the storage bytes of the string. In Excel's DBCS language editions, East Asian characters occupy two bytes while ASCII occupies one; in single-byte editions every character is one byte, making LENB identical to LEN.

howToSteps.name: Select the text
howToSteps.text: Click the cell with the text to measure.

limitations: In Excel on single-byte systems LENB always equals LEN, so it is only useful in DBCS locales.
Google Sheets counts bytes using UTF-8, where many non-ASCII characters are 2-3 bytes, differing from Excel's DBCS behavior.
Does not count formatting or formula length, only the resulting text value.

commonErrors.cause: Running Excel in a single-byte locale where every character is one byte.
commonErrors.fix: Use the difference LENB-LEN only on DBCS-enabled Excel, or rely on Google Sheets' UTF-8 counts for web data.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: In Google Sheets, LENB counts bytes using UTF-8 encoding, so non-ASCII characters such as Chinese typically count as 3 bytes each.
googleSheetsEquivalent.notes: Sheets returns 6 for "你好" (UTF-8, 3 bytes per character), unlike DBCS Excel which returns 4.

faq.question: When does LENB differ from LEN?
faq.answer: Only for multi-byte (DBCS) characters in a DBCS edition of Excel; otherwise they are equal.

faq.question: How does Google Sheets handle LENB?
faq.answer: Sheets uses UTF-8 byte counts, so East Asian characters usually count as 3 bytes each.

faq.question: Why would I use LENB?
faq.answer: To detect or handle multi-byte character data when processing DBCS text.
